exam-09-q01.why_correct_en: The flower associated with Northern Ireland is the shamrock.

exam-09-q02.why_correct_en: At Waterloo in 1815, the army led by the Duke of Wellington and its allies, supported decisively by Prussian forces, defeated Napoleon. The battle ended Napoleon's Hundred Days return to power and the phase of conflict described by the question.

exam-09-q03.why_correct_en: For the answer intended by this question, False is correct: the Bank of England currently issues £5, £10, £20 and £50 notes, so £50 is its highest denomination and there is no circulating £100 Bank of England note. However, the wording 'in the UK' is imprecise. Authorised banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland also issue sterling notes, and Bank of Scotland issues a £100 polymer note. It is therefore inaccurate to say simply that the UK has no £100 notes. The precise revision point is that £50 is the highest-value Bank of England note; read literally across all authorised UK note issues, the original question is ambiguous.

exam-09-q05.why_correct_en: If you wish to be a permanent resident or citizen of the UK, you should: respect and obey the law, look after yourself and your family, respect the rights of others, including their right to their own opinions, treat others with fairness and look after the area in which you live and the environment.

exam-09-q06.why_correct_en: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England.

exam-09-q07.why_correct_en: Women were given the right to vote at the age of 21, the same as men.

exam-09-q08.why_correct_en: Hogmanay is the Scots name for 31 December and Scotland's New Year's Eve celebrations, with written examples dating from around 1604. Its exact origin is disputed. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language considers the strongest explanation to be a borrowing, through Scotland's long connections with France, from northern French forms such as hoginane and ultimately a French New Year expression associated with a New Year's gift, a children's call for such a gift, or New Year's Eve; its latter element may reflect l'an neuf, meaning 'the New Year'. After the Scottish Reformation, Christmas celebrations were discouraged for a long period, so winter gift-giving and festivities became concentrated around New Year. Hogmanay consequently developed into a major Scottish celebration, including Auld Lang Syne and first-footing, when the first visitor after midnight traditionally brings symbolic gifts for good fortune.

exam-09-q09.why_correct_en: The capital city of Northern Ireland is Belfast.

exam-09-q11.why_correct_en: Northern Ireland uses individual electoral registration: each eligible person is responsible for registering themselves and supplying their own identifying information, rather than one head of household registering everyone at an address.

exam-09-q12.why_correct_en: Policy and laws governing defence, foreign affairs, immigration, taxation and social security all remain under central UK government control. However, many other public services, such as education, are controlled by the devolved administrations.

exam-09-q13.why_correct_en: Most citizens of the UK, the Irish republic or the Commonwealth aged 18 or over can stand for public office. There are some exceptions, including: members of the armed forces, civil servants and people found guilty of certain criminal offences.

exam-09-q14.why_correct_en: During Victorian times, the government began to promote policies of free trade, abolishing a number of taxes on imported goods. One example of this was the repealing of the Corn Laws in 1846. These had prevented the import of cheap grain. The reforms helped the development of the British industry, because raw materials could now be imported cheaply.

exam-09-q15.why_correct_en: Admiral Nelson was in charge of the British fleet at the Battle of Trafalgar against the Spanish fleet and was killed in the battle.

exam-09-q16.why_correct_en: Serfs were peasants who had a small area of their lord’s land where they could grow food.

exam-09-q17.why_correct_en: The Industrial Revolution was the rapid development of industry in Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries. Britain was the first country to industrialise on a large scale. It happened because of the development of machinery and the use of steam power.

exam-09-q18.why_correct_en: False. You can contact MPs by letter or telephone at their constituency office, or at their office in the House of Commons. In addition, many MPs, Assembly members, MSPs and MEPs hold regular local ‘surgeries’, where constituents can go in person to talk about issues that are of concern to them.

exam-09-q19.why_correct_en: The Reformation was a movement against the authority of the Pope and the ideas and practices of the Roman Catholic Church.

exam-09-q20.why_correct_en: William the Conqueror sent people all over England to draw up lists of all the towns and villages. The people who lived there, who owned the land and what animals they owned were also listed. This was called the Domesday Book.

exam-09-q21.why_correct_en: Richard Austen Butler became a Conservative MP in 1923 and held several positions before becoming responsible for education in 1941. In this role, he oversaw the introduction of the Education Act 1944 (often called ‘The Butler Act’), which introduced free secondary education in England and Wales.

exam-09-q22.why_correct_en: The small claims procedure is an informal way of helping people to settle minor disputes without spending a lot of time and money using a lawyer.

exam-09-q23.why_correct_en: In 1851, the Great Exhibition opened in Hyde Park in the Crystal Palace, a huge building made of steel and glass. Exhibits ranged from huge machines to handmade goods.

exam-09-q24.why_correct_en: Florence Nightingale was a nurse. She is often regarded as the founder of modern nursing.
